units.title: The Elements of Art
units.blurb: The seven building blocks of every picture: line, shape, form, space, value, texture and color.

units.title: Color Theory
units.blurb: Hue, value and saturation; the color wheel; tints, tones and shades; the color schemes; color temperature and contrast.

units.title: Mixing Paint and Mixing Light
units.blurb: Subtractive mixing in paint and ink, additive mixing in light, the three sets of primaries, neutrals, and print versus screen.

units.title: The Principles of Design
units.blurb: How artists arrange the elements: balance, contrast, emphasis, movement, pattern, rhythm, unity, variety and proportion.

units.title: Composition and Analysis
units.blurb: Looking at a work step by step, the structures of composition, value patterns, color schemes in paintings, and what colors mean.

topics.title: The Seven Elements of Art
topics.short: Line, shape, form, space, value, texture and color are the elements of art: the parts every picture is built from.
topics.trouble: People mix up the elements (the parts) with the principles of design (the ways the parts are arranged). Balance is a principle, not an element.

topics.title: Line as an Element
topics.short: A line is a mark longer than it is wide. Lines can be actual or implied, and they can outline, show direction and suggest movement or calm.
topics.trouble: People count only drawn lines. An implied line, like a row of dots or a person's gaze, guides the eye too.

topics.title: Shape and Form
topics.short: Shapes are flat areas, geometric or organic; forms have three dimensions, actual in sculpture or implied by shading in a picture.
topics.trouble: People call a shaded circle a shape. Once shading makes it look solid, it reads as a form.

topics.title: Space
topics.short: Space is the area around and between things: positive and negative space on the surface, and the illusion of depth in a picture.
topics.trouble: People think empty space is wasted. Negative space shapes a composition as much as the objects do.

topics.title: Value
topics.short: Value is lightness and darkness. It shows form and light and creates contrast, with or without color.
topics.trouble: People think bright colors are always light in value. A saturated blue or red can be quite dark.

topics.title: Texture: Actual and Implied
topics.short: Actual texture can be touched (thick paint, carved wood); implied texture only looks rough, smooth or soft.
topics.trouble: People think a smooth photograph of bark has actual texture. It has implied texture; the surface is flat.

topics.title: Color as an Element
topics.short: Color is what we see when light of different wavelengths reaches our eyes. Artists describe it by hue, value and saturation.
topics.trouble: People think an object has its color no matter the light. Its color depends on the light that falls on it and what it reflects.

topics.title: Hue, Value and Saturation
topics.short: Hue is the color family (red, blue). Value is how light or dark. Saturation, also called intensity or chroma, is how pure or grayed it is.
topics.trouble: People mix up value and saturation. A pale pink is light (high value) and also low in saturation; a deep navy is dark but can be fairly saturated.

topics.title: The Color Wheel
topics.short: The painter's traditional wheel puts red, yellow and blue as primaries, orange, green and violet between them, and six tertiaries in the gaps.
topics.trouble: People think the color wheel is a law of nature. It is a tool for arranging hues; different wheels (painter's, printer's, light) put different primaries at the points.

topics.title: Tertiary Colors
topics.short: A tertiary color mixes a primary with the secondary beside it. Its name puts the primary first: red-orange, yellow-green, blue-violet.
topics.trouble: People name a tertiary "orange-red" or mix two colors that are not neighbors on the wheel, like red and green.

topics.title: Tints, Tones and Shades
topics.short: A tint adds white, a shade adds black, and a tone adds gray. Each changes value or saturation but keeps the hue.
topics.trouble: People use "shade" for any version of a color. In art, a shade is the color plus black.

topics.title: Monochromatic Color
topics.short: A monochromatic scheme uses one hue with its tints, tones and shades.
topics.trouble: People think monochromatic means black and white only. Any single hue in many values is monochromatic.

topics.title: Complementary Colors
topics.short: Complements sit across from each other on the wheel: red and green, blue and orange, yellow and violet. Side by side they make each other look stronger.
topics.trouble: People pick complements from the wrong wheel: in light (RGB) the complement of blue is yellow, on the painter's wheel it is orange. Say which wheel you mean.

topics.title: Analogous Colors
topics.short: Analogous colors sit next to each other on the wheel, such as yellow, yellow-green and green. They look calm and unified.
topics.trouble: People pick colors that are near each other in a crayon box but far apart on the wheel.

topics.title: Triadic and Split-Complementary Schemes
topics.short: A triad uses three hues evenly spaced around the wheel (red, yellow, blue). A split-complementary uses one hue and the two on either side of its complement.
topics.trouble: People choose any three colors and call it a triad. On a 12-hue wheel a triad's hues are four steps apart.

topics.title: Warm, Cool and Relative Temperature
topics.short: Reds, oranges and yellows read warm; blues, greens and violets read cool. Temperature is also relative: a red can be warmer or cooler than another red.
topics.trouble: People think a color is warm or cool in itself. A violet looks warm next to blue and cool next to red.

topics.title: Colors Change Their Neighbors
topics.short: A color looks different depending on what surrounds it: the same gray looks lighter on black than on white and takes on a hint of the surrounding color's complement.
topics.trouble: People judge a color alone and are surprised when it looks different in the finished picture.

topics.title: Subtractive Mixing: Paint and Ink
topics.short: Pigments absorb (subtract) some light and reflect the rest. Mixing pigments subtracts more, so mixtures get darker and duller.
topics.trouble: People expect mixing paints to brighten a color. Every pigment added absorbs more light, so mixtures move toward dark and dull.

topics.title: Additive Mixing: Light
topics.short: Colored lights add together. Red, green and blue light are the additive primaries: red and green light make yellow, and all three make white.
topics.trouble: People expect red and green light to make brown, as paint would. Lights add, so they make yellow.

topics.title: Three Sets of Primaries: RYB, CMY and RGB
topics.short: Painters traditionally use red, yellow and blue; printers use cyan, magenta and yellow (plus black); screens and light use red, green and blue.
topics.trouble: People think there is one true set of primaries. Each set fits a different medium and color model.

topics.title: Mixing Neutrals: Browns and Grays
topics.short: Mixing a color with its complement lowers its saturation; in the right amounts complements make rich browns and grays.
topics.trouble: People reach for black to dull a color. A touch of its complement grays it while keeping it lively.

topics.title: Print and Screen
topics.short: A screen mixes tiny red, green and blue lights; a printer lays tiny dots of cyan, magenta, yellow and black on white paper.
topics.trouble: People expect a bright screen color to print exactly the same. Some screen colors are brighter than inks can reach on paper.

topics.title: Balance
topics.short: Balance is how visual weight is spread: symmetrical (mirror halves), asymmetrical (unequal things that still feel even) or radial (around a center).
topics.trouble: People think only mirror symmetry balances. A small, dark, detailed shape can balance a large, light, plain one.

topics.title: Contrast
topics.short: Contrast puts unlike things side by side: light and dark, big and small, smooth and rough, warm and cool.
topics.trouble: People think contrast means only black against white. Any strong difference, in size, texture or color, is contrast.

topics.title: Emphasis
topics.short: Emphasis makes one part stand out as the focal point, through contrast, isolation, placement, detail or lines that lead to it.
topics.trouble: People emphasize several things equally, and then nothing stands out.

topics.title: Movement
topics.short: Movement is the path the eye travels through a work, led by lines, edges, shapes and repeated colors.
topics.trouble: People think movement means a picture of something moving. In design it means the path the viewer's eye follows.

topics.title: Pattern
topics.short: A pattern repeats a motif (a shape, line or color) in a regular way across a surface.
topics.trouble: People use pattern and rhythm as the same word. A pattern is the repeated motif; rhythm is the sense of beat its spacing creates.

topics.title: Rhythm
topics.short: Rhythm is a visual beat made by repeating elements with spacing: regular, alternating, progressive (gradually changing) or flowing.
topics.trouble: People think rhythm needs exact repeats. A progressive rhythm changes step by step, like circles that grow.

topics.title: Unity and Variety
topics.short: Unity makes the parts feel like they belong together; variety adds differences to keep it interesting. Good designs balance the two.
topics.trouble: People think unity means everything the same. Too much sameness is dull; too much variety is chaos.

topics.title: Proportion and Scale
topics.short: Proportion is the size of parts compared with each other; scale is size compared with something known. Some art uses hierarchical scale: the most important figure largest.
topics.trouble: People read a large figure in older art as closer. In hierarchical scale, size shows importance, not distance.

topics.title: Looking Step by Step
topics.short: Describe what you see, analyze how the elements and principles work, interpret what it might mean, then judge with reasons.
topics.trouble: People jump straight to "I like it" or to a meaning before looking. Describe first; the evidence comes from looking.

topics.title: Triangles, Diagonals and S-Curves
topics.short: Many paintings are built on a simple structure: a stable triangle, an energetic diagonal, a winding S-curve or a circle.
topics.trouble: People look only at the subject and miss the shape of the whole arrangement underneath it.

topics.title: Thirds and Focal Points in Paintings
topics.short: Find where the strongest contrast, the lines and the gazes lead; that is the focal point, and its place on the grid shapes the mood.
topics.trouble: People assume the focal point must sit on a thirds line. Painters also center it for calm, or push it to an edge for tension.

topics.title: The Value Pattern
topics.short: Squint at a painting and it simplifies into a few big light and dark shapes. That value pattern often carries the composition.
topics.trouble: People study the colors and details first. Many compositions work, or fail, at the level of three or four big values.

topics.title: Reading Color in Paintings
topics.short: Name the scheme (complementary, analogous, triadic or monochromatic), the temperature and the saturation, and say what they do for the work.
topics.trouble: People name every color they see instead of the overall scheme and its effect.

topics.title: What Colors Mean
topics.short: Color meanings come from culture and history, not nature: white is worn for weddings in some places and for mourning in others.
topics.trouble: People think a color means the same thing everywhere. Meanings change across cultures, times and contexts.

topics.title: Readable Color: Contrast for Text
topics.short: Text needs enough value contrast with its background to read easily; web guidelines ask for a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 for normal text.
topics.trouble: People pair colors that differ in hue but are close in value, like red text on green, which is hard to read.
